sessions.name: Movement Capacity Builder
sessions.note: Avoid doing every climb with the same grip type. For example: If the first few problems use crimps, choose problems that involve slopers or pinches next. Repeating the same grip repeatedly can overload small finger joints even at moderate intensity. Spread the stress across different grips. Your fingers will thank you later.
sessions.description:
Session Intention
Accumulate a high number of quality climbing reps while maintaining excellent movement mechanics. Climb with patience and control. Your goal is not to finish climbs quickly. Your goal is to move well repeatedly. This session introduces one of the most important skills in climbing training: volume without deterioration. You will climb a series of moderate boulders around RPE 6–7. 
That means: Challenging enough that you must pay attention… but easy enough that you can maintain clean movement.
Focus on:
• quiet foot placements
• hips close to the wall
• relaxed fingers
• breathing during sequences
If your movement starts getting sloppy, slow down. The entire point of this session is to train your body to repeat good climbing over and over again. That’s what eventually lets climbers handle harder training later.
Grip Overlap Warning! Avoid doing every climb with the same grip type. For example: If the first few problems use crimps, choose problems that involve slopers or pinches next. Repeating the same grip repeatedly can overload small finger joints even at moderate intensity. Spread the stress across different grips. Your fingers will thank you later.

groups.note: Please bias toward more open handed grips during the Capacity Phase (3 Finger Drag, 4 Finger Open Hand, Slopers, Big Pinches, etc). The goal of this phase is to build your grip “engine” and increase tissue capacity through sustainable submaximal loading, not to maximize peak force through aggressive crimping. Open handed positions generally create less pulley and joint stress while still building tremendous forearm, tendon, and work capacity adaptations. Overusing high force crimp positions during this phase often shifts the stimulus away from capacity development and toward excessive structural finger loading, which can fry your fingers, increase fatigue, and raise injury risk before the higher intensity phases even begin.

Do the dynamic stretching routine

Warm-up set guidelines:

If your workout's intensity ranges are as follows, do the recommended amount of warm-up sets.

Low intensity (6-7 RPE): 1–2 warm-up sets
Moderate intensity (7-8.5 RPE): 2–3 warm-up sets
High intensity / heavy (8.5-9.5 RPE): 3–5 warm-up sets with smaller load jumps as you get heavier

sessions.name: Capacity Phase Mobility Development Day
sessions.description:
Phase 1 is about building control before range.
The goal of this phase is to establish correct positioning, active tension, and left–right symmetry in wide stances and high-step positions before chasing deeper mobility. Rather than forcing flexibility, Phase 1 teaches you how to support yourself at the edges of your current range through slow, controlled reps and isometric holds. This creates tissue tolerance, improves coordination, and reduces injury risk, setting the foundation for all deeper range, load, and speed work later in the year.

Session Intention
Build hip mobility and end-range strength that improves climbing positions. Move slowly and intentionally. This is not a stretching session — it’s strength training for mobility.
These exercises train positions that climbers constantly struggle with:
• high feet
• wide stances
• drop knees
• compression positions

Instead of forcing flexibility, you are teaching your body to control these positions under load. Move slowly. Pause in the end ranges. Focus on breathing and balance.
When this work is done consistently, climbers often notice that:
• high steps feel easier
• hips stay closer to the wall
• tension becomes easier to maintain

sessions.name: Skill Practice + Density Hangs
sessions.note:
This is a big one. Because you are already loading the fingers with Density Hangs, you need to be smart about grip overlap in the climbing and pull work around it.

A few rules:
	•	Your density hangs are on an edge, avoid making the rest of the session heavily edge-dominant.
	•	If the skill drill or free climbing is already crimp-heavy, choose a more open-hand or varied grip for the hangs if possible.
	•	Avoid stacking repeated half crimp stress across the entire day.
	•	If fingers feel stiff, puffy, or irritated during the hangs, reduce the intensity immediately or skip them.

The goal is distributed stress, not hammering the exact same tissues over and over.

Think:
	•	edges + slopers
	•	open hand + pinch
	•	varied movement + submax hang loading

That is how you build finger capacity without accidentally turning a capacity day into the beginning of a finger issue.
sessions.description:
Session Intention

Build finger and tissue capacity through submaximal finger loading while continuing to improve movement skill on the wall. Stay controlled and patient. This is not a max strength day. Your job is to build capacity, accumulate quality reps, and leave your fingers feeling worked, not irritated.

This day combines movement practice with one of the most important finger-loading tools in the entire Capacity Phase: Density Hangs.

That matters because this phase is not about testing how strong your fingers are. It’s about teaching them to tolerate repeatable loading. The session starts with your assigned skill drill so you can sharpen movement quality while fresh.

Then you move into either:
Density Hangs, or
Free Climbing (at a low intensity if your fingers are too fatigued for Density Hangs)

If you are doing Density Hangs, the goal is simple: Build finger capacity through controlled, submaximal time under tension.

That means:

no grinding
no shaking
no ugly form
no “let’s see how much I can survive” energy

You should be using a hold size and intensity that lets you stay smooth and repeatable. The point is to give the fingers, pulleys, and connective tissue a consistent signal that says: “Get better at handling load.” Not: “Emergency. Panic. Survive this hang.”

If you are doing the Free Climbing version instead, the same rule applies. Climb in that RPE 5–6 zone where you can still focus on precision, body position, and efficient movement.
Then finish with the assigned Pull session, keeping the quality high and the ego low. This day should leave you feeling like you trained. Not like you got away with something.

sessions.name: Recovery + Optional Stretching
sessions.description:
Today is a rest day, but gentle movement can still be beneficial if it supports recovery rather than adding fatigue. A brief dynamic warm-up followed by relaxed static stretching can help increase blood flow, reduce residual muscle tension, and restore comfortable ranges of motion without stressing the nervous system. This combination supports tissue hydration, improves joint comfort, and can enhance relaxation and parasympathetic recovery, often leaving you feeling looser, calmer, and more refreshed for the days ahead. The goal is not to push flexibility or create strain, but to move easily, breathe well, and support overall recovery.

These static stretches have been intentionally selected to complement and support the hip mobility work you are doing throughout the program. Feel free to do this routine 5-6 days per week.

sessions.description:
Session Intention
Introduce slightly higher-intensity climbing while maintaining excellent movement quality and control. The goal of this session is to begin nudging intensity upward without sacrificing efficiency, coordination, or finger health.
Seek out a wide range of boulders that expose your biggest opportunities for improvement—different wall angles, hold types, movement styles, and body positions. This spreads the mechanical load across the fingers, shoulders, core, and lower body while developing more complete climbing ability.
Commit fully to each move and climb with purpose, but avoid desperate attempts, excessive fighting, or repeated failures. You should be operating at an intensity where the moves feel challenging and engaging, yet still allow you to execute them with precision, timing, and control.
Think of this session as high-quality problem solving under moderate stress—training your body and brain to perform difficult climbing movements while staying composed, efficient, and technically sharp.

sessions.name: Capacity Phase Mobility Development Day
sessions.description:
Phase 1 is about building control before range.
The goal of this phase is to establish correct positioning, active tension, and left–right symmetry in wide stances and high-step positions before chasing deeper mobility. Rather than forcing flexibility, Phase 1 teaches you how to support yourself at the edges of your current range through slow, controlled reps and isometric holds. This creates tissue tolerance, improves coordination, and reduces injury risk, setting the foundation for all deeper range, load, and speed work later in the year.

Session Intention
Build hip mobility and end-range strength that improves climbing positions. Move slowly and intentionally. This is not a stretching session — it’s strength training for mobility.
These exercises train positions that climbers constantly struggle with:
• high feet
• wide stances
• drop knees
• compression positions

Instead of forcing flexibility, you are teaching your body to control these positions under load. Move slowly. Pause in the end ranges. Focus on breathing and balance.
When this work is done consistently, climbers often notice that:
• high steps feel easier
• hips stay closer to the wall
• tension becomes easier to maintain

sessions.note:

	•	Avoid stacking repeated half crimp stress across the entire day.
	•	If fingers feel stiff, puffy, or irritated during the hangs, reduce the intensity immediately or skip them.

	•	edges + slopers

sessions.name: End of Week Reflection + Stretch
sessions.description:
Today is a rest day, but gentle movement can still be beneficial if it supports recovery rather than adding fatigue. A brief dynamic warm-up followed by relaxed static stretching can help increase blood flow, reduce residual muscle tension, and restore comfortable ranges of motion without stressing the nervous system. This combination supports tissue hydration, improves joint comfort, and can enhance relaxation and parasympathetic recovery, often leaving you feeling looser, calmer, and more refreshed for the days ahead. The goal is not to push flexibility or create strain, but to move easily, breathe well, and support overall recovery.

These static stretches have been intentionally selected to complement and support the hip mobility work you are doing throughout the program. Feel free to do this routine 5-6 days per week.

sessions.description:
Static Stretching – Guidelines & Best Practices

Warm Up Properly

Always begin with a thorough warm-up before static stretching. Static stretching should only be performed when tissues are already warm.

Effective warm-up options include:

Light climbing
Dynamic hip mobility
Joint circles (hips, knees, ankles)
Easy aerobic movement

The goal is to increase blood flow and reduce tissue stiffness before holding stretches.

Stretch Intensity & Execution

Move slowly into each stretch until you feel moderate tension, not pain.
Static stretching should feel controlled and relaxed, not forced.
Avoid pushing deeper aggressively; allow range to improve through relaxation.

Each stretch should be held at a consistent intensity for the full duration.

Breathing Focus
Use slow, controlled breathing throughout each stretch.
Emphasize longer exhales to reduce muscular guarding and allow deeper relaxation.
Do not hold your breath or brace excessively.

Sets & Timing

Perform 2 sets per stretch
Hold each stretch for 30 seconds
Rest briefly between sets as needed

Follow the prescription exactly—more is not better during static stretching.

Focus on Technique

Maintain proper alignment for each stretch.
Avoid compensations such as spinal rounding, pelvic shifting, or knee collapse.
Quality of position matters more than depth.

Listen to Your Body

Mild discomfort or stretching sensation is normal.
Sharp pain, joint pinching, or numbness is a signal to stop and adjust.
If something feels off, reduce depth or exit the stretch.

Avoid Overstretching

Stretching aggressively does not improve flexibility faster and increases injury risk.
Progress comes from consistent, relaxed exposure, not forcing range.

Frequency & Consistency

If motivation or time is limited:

Complete at least one set of each stretch
Consistency matters more than volume

Even minimal, regular static stretching produces meaningful improvements over time.

Key Reminder

Static stretching is about relaxation and tissue tolerance, not effort or intensity.
Move slowly, breathe deeply, and prioritize quality over depth.

sessions.description:
Session Intention
Accumulate a high number of quality climbing reps while maintaining excellent movement mechanics. Climb with patience and control. Your goal is not to finish climbs quickly. Your goal is to move well repeatedly. This session introduces one of the most important skills in climbing training: volume without deterioration. You will climb a series of moderate boulders around RPE 6–7. 
That means: Challenging enough that you must pay attention… but easy enough that you can maintain clean movement.
Focus on:
• quiet foot placements
• hips close to the wall
• relaxed fingers
• breathing during sequences
If your movement starts getting sloppy, slow down. The entire point of this session is to train your body to repeat good climbing over and over again. That’s what eventually lets climbers handle harder training later.
Grip Overlap Warning! Avoid doing every climb with the same grip type. For example: If the first few problems use crimps, choose problems that involve slopers or pinches next. Repeating the same grip repeatedly can overload small finger joints even at moderate intensity. Spread the stress across different grips. Your fingers will thank you later.

exercises.name: Capacity Phase Warning!
exercises.note: I have seen far too many climbers push too hard and get minimal results and even get injured, from pushing too hard during the Capacity Phase. Please read this and commit it to memory. Leave you EGO at the door!

groups.note: Please bias toward more open handed grips during the Capacity Phase (3 Finger Drag, 4 Finger Open Hand, Slopers, Big Pinches, etc). The goal of this phase is to build your grip “engine” and increase tissue capacity through sustainable submaximal loading, not to maximize peak force through aggressive crimping. Open handed positions generally create less pulley and joint stress while still building tremendous forearm, tendon, and work capacity adaptations. Overusing high force crimp positions during this phase often shifts the stimulus away from capacity development and toward excessive structural finger loading, which can fry your fingers, increase fatigue, and raise injury risk before the higher intensity phases even begin.
